subject: Microbiology
subtopic: Erythroid tropism, fifth disease, aplastic crisis and pregnancy
concept: Parvovirus B19 is a small DNA virus with marked tropism for erythroid precursor cells and is especially important in hematology.

content.definition: Parvovirus B19 usually causes mild illness but can suppress erythropoiesis and cause transient aplastic crisis in patients with underlying hemolytic anemia.
content.explanation: The virus infects erythroid progenitor cells in bone marrow, producing transient suppression of red-cell production.
content.mechanism: Temporary cessation of erythropoiesis is usually tolerated in healthy people but can cause severe reticulocytopenia and anemia when red-cell survival is already shortened.
content.structure: Parvovirus B19 is a small non-enveloped single-stranded DNA virus.
content.function: Erythroid-cell tropism explains its major hematologic manifestations.
effects: Erythema infectiosum with a slapped-cheek rash
Transient aplastic crisis in underlying hemolytic disorders
Fetal anemia or hydrops after maternal infection
content.diagnosis: Typical fifth disease is often diagnosed clinically; PCR and serology are useful in selected hematologic, pregnancy or immunocompromised cases.
content.treatment: Treatment is generally supportive. Severe aplastic crisis may require transfusion and supportive care; persistent infection in immunocompromised patients requires specialist management.
high_yield: Parvovirus B19 targets erythroid precursor cells
Aplastic crisis is important in chronic hemolytic anemia
Pregnancy infection can cause fetal anemia and hydrops

terminology.etymology: Erythema means redness; infectiosum refers to infection.
Transient means temporary; aplastic means failure of cell production.
terminology.notes: Important complication in chronic hemolytic anemia.

yemen_context.relevance: Highly relevant to hematology because of erythroid precursor tropism; no unsupported Yemen-specific incidence is asserted.

review_notes: Original synthesis based on CDC Parvovirus B19 guidance.
